body: Regression is a human-made family of statistical estimation methods that fit a mathematical model to observed data to quantify the relationship between a dependent (outcome) variable and one or more independent (predictor) variables, yielding fitted parameters usable for prediction and inference. Parameters: (1) model form — linear, polynomial, generalized (e.g., logistic), or nonlinear; (2) estimation criterion — ordinary least squares, maximum likelihood, or regularized variants (ridge, lasso); (3) data layout — the outcome variable, the predictor variables, and the sample; (4) the working assumptions the fit makes about the error structure, which the method estimates rather than verifies. Regression is thereby distinguished from its diagnostic machinery: it produces the fitted model and its parameters, while residual analysis and influence measures are tools applied afterwards to evaluate the fit. Its persistence mechanism is teaching and re-implementation: textbooks, statistical software, and every predictive or inferential task re-instantiate the family for each new analyst; the forms extend whenever a new criterion or model family is added. [formal: regressio quantitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.25]

minimum-phase-filter is a human-made filter class defined by the property that its phase response is the minimum possible for its magnitude response, equivalently having all zeros and poles inside the unit circle for discrete-time or in left half-plane for continuous-time, causal and stable. Parameters are filter order, magnitude response specification, zero/pole locations, and implementation type. It persists through formal DSP theory, textbook codification, and repeated implementation in audio processing libraries and hardware designs. [formal: filter | substrate: matter | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.14]

Falsifiability is a human-made epistemological criterion that demarcates scientific claims from non-scientific ones by requiring that every scientific theory admit of at least one conceivable observation that could count against it. Parameters: (1) the theory or hypothesis being evaluated, (2) the set of possible observations that would contradict it, (3) the observational or experimental framework within which contradiction is determinable. Persistence mechanism: persists through philosophy of science textbooks (Popper, Lakatos, Kuhn), scientific methodology courses, peer-review standards that implicitly apply falsification reasoning, and institutional research funding criteria that require falsifiable proposals. [formal: falsabilitas | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An information-theoretic criterion for statistical model selection, defined by the formula AIC = 2k − 2ln(L), where k is the number of estimated parameters in the model and L is the maximized likelihood. The criterion estimates the relative information loss when a given model is used to represent the process that generated the data; lower AIC values indicate less estimated loss. It balances goodness-of-fit (via log-likelihood) against model complexity (via the penalty term 2k), automating the trade-off between underfitting and overfitting. Computed by evaluating each candidate model's log-likelihood at its maximum-likelihood estimates, counting its free parameters, and applying the formula. Published by Hirotugu Akaike in 1974 as derived from Kullback–Leibler divergence, it persists through statistical textbooks, software implementations (R, Python, MATLAB), and research practice across disciplines including econometrics, ecology, signal processing, and machine learning. [formal: AIC | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.10]

A butterworth-filter is a human-made filter design — the classic maximally-flat (zero-ripple) magnitude response — defined by its parameters: (1) order N, the number of pole pairs, fixing roll-off beyond cutoff at 20N dB/decade; (2) cutoff frequency wc, where the gain falls to 1/sqrt(2) (-3 dB); (3) the prototype magnitude |H(jw)| = 1/sqrt(1 + (w/wc)^(2N)), whose N poles lie on a left-half s-plane semicircle (for the digital IIR realization, mapped inside the unit circle in the z-plane by the bilinear transform). It persists as the named reference design in every DSP textbook and filter-design toolkit: the standard analog prototype from which digital IIR filters are derived by bilinear transform or impulse invariance, and the flatness yardstick against which Chebyshev and elliptic designs are compared. [formal: filtrum butterworthianum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.75]

Log-likelihood is the natural logarithm of the likelihood function, which evaluates the probability of observed data given a statistical model and its parameters; it is parameterized by the data set, the probability model (including unknown parameters), and persists as a core computational quantity in maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian inference, hypothesis testing, and model selection criteria. [formal: mathematical | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

A statistical estimator is a rule mapping a sample of observed data (random variables) to an estimate of an unknown quantity — a parameter of, or functional of, the data-generating distribution; a point estimator maps to a single value, an interval estimator to a set with a coverage level. Its parameters are the sample, the target estimand, and the assumed sampling distribution. It persists because its performance is formally evaluable against the sampling distribution — bias, variance, mean squared error, consistency, asymptotic normality, sufficiency, efficiency — which makes it the unit of comparison in estimation theory: the theorems of the discipline (Cramér–Rao bound, Lehmann–Scheffé, asymptotics of maximum-likelihood estimation) are stated about estimators as a class, and specific estimators (maximum likelihood, minimum-variance unbiased, Bayes, method of moments) are named instances of this kind.

Phase-locked vocoder is a human-made audio signal processing algorithm that modifies the horizontal phase progression between successive STFT frames to preserve phase coherence across frequency bins, reducing phasiness artifacts in time-stretching and pitch-shifting. Parameters: (1) analysis/synthesis window length and hop size; (2) pitch period estimate per frame; (3) phase locking rule — a threshold on inter-frame phase deviation that forces phase continuity by adjusting synthesis phase; (4) frequency bin grouping for phase propagation; (5) synthesis overlap-add parameters. Persistence mechanism: documented in audio engineering literature and DSP textbooks; implemented in reference DSP libraries, audio plug-ins, and real-time audio frameworks; coefficients and rules stored in software code and parameter presets. [formal: vocoder phase-lockus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

A statistical technique that combines predictions from multiple candidate models by computing a weighted average, rather than selecting a single best model. Given m candidate models with predictions f_i(x) and non-negative weights w_i summing to 1, the averaged prediction at input x is Σ_{i=1}^{m} w_i · f_i(x). The weights are typically derived from a model selection criterion such as AIC: w_i = exp(−Δ_i / 2) / Σ_j exp(−Δ_j / 2), where Δ_i is the difference between model i's AIC and the minimum AIC across all candidates. Model averaging reduces selection uncertainty and often produces more accurate predictions than any individual model, especially when no single model is clearly superior. Computed by evaluating each candidate model, deriving weights from a criterion, and forming the weighted sum. Established in statistical practice through Burnham and Anderson (2002) and earlier Bayesian model averaging (Raftery et al., 1997), it persists through statistical textbooks, software packages (R's MuMIn, AICcmodavg), and research practice across ecology, econometrics, climate science, and machine learning. [formal: MA | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 2.11]

A typology is a human-made systematic classification scheme that organizes a domain of phenomena into distinct, mutually exclusive types based on shared structural or functional characteristics. Parameters: (1) the classification criteria (dimensions along which types differ), (2) the set of types defined by particular combinations of criteria values, (3) the exhaustiveness condition (whether all cases in the domain must be classifiable), (4) the criteria's independence (whether dimensions can co-vary or must be orthogonal). Persistence mechanism: persists through academic taxonomies, classification standards, research methodology frameworks, and the conceptual schemas embedded in disciplinary training; re-instantiated whenever a new domain requires systematic categorization. A typology is distinguished from a simple list by its systematic criteria and from a hierarchy by its typically flat or multi-dimensional type space rather than a single parent-child tree. [formal: typologia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

A Butterworth filter is a human-made analog or digital filter design characterized by maximally flat frequency response in the passband, with no ripples. Parameters: (1) filter order N (determines rolloff steepness of 20·N dB/decade), (2) cutoff frequency fc (3 dB point where response drops), (3) passband ripple (zero by design), (4) stopband attenuation profile. A Butterworth filter of order N has all poles placed on a semicircle in the left half of the s-plane at equal angular intervals, yielding the flat magnitude response |H(f)|² = 1/(1+(f/fc)^(2N)). Persistence mechanism: persists through filter design textbooks (Sedra/Smith, Oppenheim), standard electronic component catalogs, SPICE model libraries, DSP implementation toolkits (MATLAB's filter design, SciPy's scipy.signal.butter), and analog circuit design handbooks. [formal: butterworth | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Sustainability is a human-made principle or practice aimed at maintaining systems, processes, or resource use at levels that can be perpetuated over time without depleting natural capital or exceeding ecological carrying capacity. Parameters: (1) the system boundary (what is being sustained — ecosystem, economy, organization, practice), (2) the time horizon (short-term operational vs. long-term intergenerational), (3) the resource constraints (renewable vs. non-renewable inputs, waste output limits), (4) the maintenance mechanism (regulation, market incentive, technology, behavior change). Persistence mechanism: persists through policy frameworks, corporate ESG reporting standards, certification systems (e.g., LEED, B Corp), research literature, and institutionalized assessment methodologies; instantiated whenever a decision requires evaluation of long-term viability against short-term gain. [formal: sustentatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Cherry-pick is a human-made version-control operation that selects and applies specific commits from one branch to another without merging the entire source branch. Parameters: (1) source commit hashes to be selected, (2) target branch onto which they are applied, (3) conflict resolution strategy when the target branch has divergent history, (4) commit message override or preservation flag. Persistence mechanism: stored as new commit objects in the version-control repository, recorded in branch history and reflog; persists through repository state, CI/CD audit trails, and developer workflow documentation. [formal: ceras electio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

The sampling theorem (Nyquist-Shannon) is a stated result of mathematical analysis: a continuous-time signal bandlimited to B hertz is completely determined, and exactly reconstructible, by its samples taken at any rate exceeding 2B hertz (the Nyquist rate), via sinc interpolation. Parameters: (1) bandwidth B of the signal, (2) sampling rate fs in samples per second, (3) Nyquist rate 2B as the minimum alias-free sampling rate, (4) the reconstruction kernel (sinc / ideal lowpass interpolation). Persistence mechanism: proved by Fourier-analytic methods and sustained in DSP textbooks, engineering curricula, and analog-to-digital design practice, where the choice of sampling rate is a decision grounded in this theorem. [formal: theorema nyquist-shannon | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Mask-based enhancement is a human-made signal-processing technique that improves speech quality by estimating a time-frequency mask to selectively attenuate noise while preserving speech components. Parameters: (1) mask type — ideal ratio mask, binary mask, soft mask, or learned mask, (2) estimation method — statistical estimator, Wiener filter, deep neural network, (3) time-frequency representation — STFT window length, hop size, window function, (4) decision threshold or sparsity constraint, (5) application rule — multiplication in magnitude domain with phase preservation or complex mask. Persistence mechanism: persists through speech enhancement research literature, telecommunications standards, hearing-aid firmware, and software libraries that implement mask estimation and application; re-instantiated whenever a new speech enhancement system requires selective time-frequency suppression. [formal: enhancement mascatus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

A vocoder that synthesizes speech by modeling and resynthesizing the vocal tract's formant frequencies — the resonant peaks of the speech spectrum. Parameters: input audio signal, formant detection algorithm (e.g., linear prediction analysis), formant frequency tracks, bandwidth parameters, and amplitude envelopes for each formant band. Persistence mechanism: software implementation of the formant analysis-synthesis pipeline, typically realized through digital signal processing algorithms that extract formant parameters from speech and reconstruct them via excitation-source filtering. The output preserves the perceptual qualities of voiced speech while enabling pitch and duration control independent of the original source. [formal: formant-vocoder | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A state-space model is a mathematical representation of a system as a set of first-order evolution equations: ẋ = f(x, u, t) for the state dynamics (where x is the state vector, u is the input vector, and f maps states and inputs to state derivatives) and y = h(x, u, t) for the output equation (where y is the output vector and h maps states and inputs to outputs), with persistence grounded in the state-variable formalism that reduces higher-order differential equations to coupled first-order form, enabling analysis of multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems, stability via eigenvalues of the Jacobian ∂f/∂x, and optimal estimation via recursive algorithms such as the Kalman filter (Law 6, trailer).

A statistical divergence is a mathematical function D[P||Q] that takes two probability distributions P and Q over the same sample space and returns a non-negative real number measuring how dissimilar they are, with D[P||Q]=0 if and only if P=Q almost everywhere; it is parameterized by a generating functional or integral form (e.g. f-divergence via a convex function f, R\'enyi divergence via a real parameter α, Tsallis divergence via a real parameter q), and it persists as an abstracted class of functionals on the space of probability measures, distinguished by properties such as convexity, triangle inequality failure, and information-geometric monotonicity (Law 6, trailer).

new_sustainability is a framework for evaluating and redesigning industrial and economic systems to operate within planetary boundaries while maintaining development goals. Parameters: (1) planetary boundaries — the nine ecological limits (climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen/phosphorus cycles, freshwater use, land use, ocean acidification, atmospheric aerosol loading, chemical pollution, ozone depletion) that define the safe operating space; (2) development goals — the UN Sustainable Development Goals that define the human aspirations to be met; (3) time horizon — the decadal scale at which transitions must occur; (4) material flow accounting — the quantitative tracking of energy, water, and raw materials through economic systems. Persistence mechanism: tracked through institutional reports (UN SDSN Sustainable Development Reports, IPCC assessments), corporate sustainability disclosures (GRI, SASB standards), and policy frameworks (Paris Agreement, EU Green Deal). [formal: novum-sustentabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

Spectral flatness measure is a metric computed as the ratio of the geometric mean to the arithmetic mean of a power spectrum, quantifying the noisiness of a signal; parameters include window length, hop size, and frequency band, and it persists as an algorithmic definition in digital signal processing literature and audio analysis software libraries. [formal: mathematical | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

A Wiener filter is a human-made optimal linear filter that estimates a desired signal from noisy observations by minimizing the mean-squared error between the estimate and the target. Parameters: (1) the signal and noise power spectral densities S_x(f), S_n(f) — the frequency-domain solution is H(f) = S_x(f) / (S_x(f) + S_n(f)), so the a priori signal-to-noise ratio profile sets the gain at each frequency; (2) the filter structure — a frequency-domain transfer function, or a time-domain tap set solved from the Wiener–Hopf normal equations (FIR or IIR realization); (3) the statistical assumptions — joint second-order stationarity, within which the Wiener solution is the best LINEAR estimator (optimal within the linear class, not necessarily overall); (4) the adaptation regime — a fixed steady-state design, or an adaptive approximation (LMS/RLS) tracking non-stationary spectra. Persistence mechanism: persists as the canonical solution of the linear minimum-mean-squared-error problem in signal-processing textbooks, as a standard stage in speech-enhancement and audio-deconvolution toolchains, in communications receiver filtering and geophysical Wiener deconvolution, and as the limit that Kalman filtering generalizes in the time domain. [formal: filtrum optimum | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.04]

Butterworth filter is a human-made signal-processing filter type designed to have a maximally flat magnitude response in the passband, with no ripples. Parameters: (1) filter order N (determines roll-off steepness at -20N dB/decade in the stopband), (2) cutoff frequency fc (the -3 dB point where response drops to 1/√2 of passband gain), (3) filter type — low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, or band-stop, (4) passband ripple tolerance (zero by design — the Butterworth characteristic is maximally flat). The transfer function has all poles evenly spaced on a semicircle in the left half of the s-plane (analog) or mapped to the z-plane (digital). Unlike Chebyshev or elliptic filters, it sacrifices roll-off steepness for a monotonic, ripple-free response. Persistence mechanism: stored as coefficient arrays in DSP libraries, filter-design toolkits (MATLAB, SciPy, GNU Radio), and embedded audio processing systems; persists through textbook implementations, standardized filter-design tables, and audio engineering practice where flat passband response is prioritized over selectivity. [formal: butterworthianum filtrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Phase coherence is a human-made signal-processing property that quantifies the consistency of phase relationships across frequency components or over time in a signal. Parameters: (1) the phase relationship metric between frequency bins or time frames, typically measured as the correlation of instantaneous phase, (2) the analysis window length and hop size used to estimate coherence, (3) the reference signal or baseline against which phase deviation is judged, (4) the coherence threshold defining acceptable consistency. Persistence mechanism: persists through DSP textbooks, audio analysis software libraries, speech and music processing research, and measurement instruments that report inter-channel or inter-band phase coherence; re-instantiated whenever a new analysis or synthesis task requires phase alignment assessment. [formal: cohaerentia phase | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A formant vocoder is a human-made signal-processing technique that analyzes speech into a small set of formant frequencies, bandwidths, and excitation parameters, and synthesizes speech from them. Parameters: (1) number of formants tracked per frame, (2) formant frequency trajectories F1...Fn and bandwidths B1...Bn extracted from the speech spectrum, (3) excitation model — voiced pulse train or unvoiced noise, (4) gain envelope per frame. Persistence: the technique persists through speech-synthesis textbooks, historical vocoder hardware (Chowning, Dudley), and modern speech-coding and voice-conversion research that re-implements formant tracking and synthesis. [formal: vocator formans | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A probit-model is a regression technique for binary dependent variables where the latent variable y* is modeled as a linear combination of predictors (y* = Xβ + ε) with ε ~ N(0,1), and the observed binary outcome y equals 1 when y* > 0 and 0 otherwise. The probability P(y=1|x) = Φ(Xβ) where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (the probit link). Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood. The model persists through statistical software implementations (R's glm family=binomial(link='probit'), Python's statsmodels Probit, Stata's probit) and its formal statement in econometric and biostatistical textbooks. [formal: probit-model | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.45]

A vocoder is a human-made signal-processing technique that analyzes an audio signal into a compact parametric representation, manipulates that representation, and synthesizes a new signal from it. Parameters: (1) the analysis stage decomposing the signal into components - classically a glottal source plus a vocal-tract filter, in spectral vocoders a frame of STFT magnitude and phase; (2) the transmitted or stored parameter set - spectral envelope plus excitation, or per-frame spectral coefficients; (3) the synthesis stage reconstructing output from the parameters. Two founding lines persist: source-filter vocoders (Fletcher and Flatte, 1928-1972), which encode the voice as excitation plus envelope, and spectral and phase vocoders (Flatte 1972; the phase vocoder), which encode the signal as modified STFT frames. Persistence: the DSP literature, speech-coder standards, and the audio-effects market in hardware units and DAW plugins. [formal: vocator | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Formalism is a human-made philosophical and mathematical approach that treats theoretical systems as compositions of formal symbols manipulated according to explicit rules, independent of semantic interpretation. Parameters: (1) the formal system's alphabet of symbols, (2) the formation rules governing well-formed formulas, (3) the inference or transformation rules for deriving theorems, (4) the axiom set from which derivations begin. Persistence mechanism: persists through mathematical logic textbooks, proof theory literature, computer science type systems, and automated theorem provers; formalized in systems like ZFC set theory, Peano arithmetic, and lambda calculus; maintained by mathematical communities and institutionalized in formal verification tools. [formal: formalismus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An objective metric that quantifies the perceptual difference between two utterances by computing the root-mean-square deviation of their mel-cepstral coefficient vectors in the mel-frequency domain. Parameters: reference_coefficients (finite sequence of real-valued mel-cepstral coefficients), comparison_coefficients (finite sequence of mel-cepstral coefficients of matching length and dimension), coefficient_count (positive integer specifying the number of cepstral coefficients per frame). Persistence: specified in ITU-T P.56 and ETSI TS 103 197 speech quality standards, implemented in open-source evaluation toolkits (HTS toolkit, WORLD vocoder utilities, OpenSMILE), and published in peer-reviewed audio engineering literature including ICASSP and SLT proceedings. Displayed as a single non-negative real value expressed in mel-scale distance units, where higher values indicate greater perceptual distortion.

Differential entropy is the extension of Shannon entropy to continuous probability distributions, defined as the negative integral of the probability density function times the logarithm of that density over the sample space; parameters are the continuous probability density function and its support, and it persists as a fundamental quantity in information theory, coding theory for continuous channels, and statistical mechanics. [formal: mathematical | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

Mel-cepstral distortion (MCD) is an objective metric that approximates the perceptual spectral difference between a reference utterance and a processed or synthesized utterance by comparing their mel-frequency cepstral coefficient vectors frame by frame. For each aligned frame pair, with c_i the processed-utterance coefficients and r_i the reference coefficients (typically i = 1..L with L = 12 or 13; the 0th coefficient c_0, overall level, is excluded or weighted), MCD(frame) = 10·log10( sqrt( sum_i (c_i - r_i)^2 / sum_i r_i^2 ) ) dB, and the reported value is the average over the overlapping frames. Parameters: (1) coefficient order range L, (2) c_0 treatment (excluded or weighted), (3) frame alignment and overlap interval. Persistence: standardized objective metric for TTS and speech-enhancement evaluation in the ITU-T P.56 lineage, implemented in the HTS toolkit, WORLD vocoder utilities, and OpenSMILE, and routinely reported in dB in the ICASSP and SLT speech-synthesis literature. [formal: distortio cepstralis mel | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A trope is a human-made figure of speech or rhetorical device that departs from ordinary literal meaning to produce a specific effect. Parameters: (1) the literal sense of the words used, (2) the figurative or non-literal sense produced, (3) the mechanism of departure (similarity, contiguity, substitution, or contradiction), (4) the intended rhetorical or aesthetic effect. Persistence mechanism: persists through rhetorical handbooks, literary criticism, composition pedagogy, and the accumulated usage of natural language itself; taught as a discrete category of non-literal expression and referenced in discourse analysis. The term also extends beyond rhetoric to cultural studies (where a trope is a recurring theme or motif in narrative and popular culture), but the core definition covers its classical rhetorical sense. [formal: tropus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

An f-divergence is a statistical divergence D_f[P||Q] between two probability distributions P and Q over the same sample space, defined as the expectation E_Q[f(dP/dQ)] where f is a fixed strictly convex function with f(1)=0 and dP/dQ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of P with respect to Q; specific choices of f yield specific divergences — f(t)=t log t gives KL-divergence, f(t)=(√t-1)² gives Hellinger distance, f(t)=(t-1)² gives χ²-divergence — and all f-divergences share the data-processing inequality: for any stochastic map T, D_f[P∘T⁻¹ || Q∘T⁻¹] ≤ D_f[P||Q], with persistence grounded in the convexity of f and the integral structure of probability measures (Law 6, trailer).

Any convention, rule, or agreement that facilitates coordination and interoperability within a given domain. This domain may be technical, social, economic, or cultural. Standards are maintained through a combination of formal ratification processes (e.g., ISO standards), informal adoption (e.g., common language), and the practical benefits derived from adherence. The persistence mechanism is reliant on the ongoing utility of the standard — if a standard ceases to be useful, it will be superseded by a more effective alternative.

[formal: Normae Concordiae | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.20]
